messages.subject: cluster variable
messages.body_plain:

I'm analyzing bilateral asymmetry using facial 3D images (object symmetry).

Thanks in advanced.

Best regards,

Julia Ratowiecki
PhD Candidate
Universidad de Buenos Aires, Argentina.

messages.body_plain:
Julia,

I am sorry but from your description I cannot advise how to proceed, as I do not understand what you mean that "I have individuals from the same family and I want to adjust for it by adding "family" as a cluster."

If you are thinking about having family as a random factor in the Procrustes ANOVA that evaluates asymmetry parameters (i.e. individual, side, with replicates for measurement error etc) you would need to build this ANOVA model yourself using procD.lm. This is certainly possible. A look to the help file of procD.lm and (maybe more so) to the help and vignettes of lm.rrpp in the RRPP package, would help.

But if what you want is to compare FA levels across families that is a whole different story. In that case, I would first run bilat.symmetry, then extract individual asymmetry indices (and if you want the asymmetric shape component, although I am not completely sure what a comparison of that component might tell you biologically) and then use lm.rrpp to run a model with level of asymmetry as the response variable, and family as the predictor.

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Ellen,

It’s not a coincidence. The mean shape will be identical for both.

For your second question, I would not perform allometry first and then species comparisons on the size-adjusted shapes. That is the incorrect model, and assumes that the allometry trajectories are the same for each species. Instead do:

LM  <- coords ~ size*species

The interaction of size:species is the slopes test. If significant, that means pairwise comparisons should be for comparing allometry slopes, not species means.  If this is not significant, drop the interaction term and run the model:

LM2 <- cords ~ size + species

Then do pairwise tests of size-adjusted group means.

Dean

Mike

Mshape: yes. If one looks at the code is it just finding the mean for each coordinate.

Dear all,

We are seeking a PhD student in evolutionary morphometrics at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, including research stays at University of California, Berkeley.

The student will be embedded in a team of computational scientists working on the mathematics of differential geometry and shape transformation, and biologists working on applied phylogenetics. messages.body_plain:
Jasmine,

I’m not sure what you mean by “correct the PLS that it runs for phylogeny” if you think phylo.integration does not do that.  I’ll show you an example below and then try to explain how phylo.integration works so you can decide whether the method is appropriately correcting for phylogeny.  As an example with the plethspecies data (from the phylo.integration example):

data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land)    #GPA-alignment
land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B")

IT<- phylo.integration(Y.gpa$coords,partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=land.gps,
                       phy=plethspecies$phy,iter=999)

# predicted shapes at PLS1 extremes

preds <- shape.predictor(IT$A1, IT$XScores[,1], method = "PLS",
                         pmin = min(IT$XScores[,1]),
                         pmax = max(IT$XScores[,1]),
                         pref  = 0) # an X-score of 0 is where the reference is found

plotRefToTarget(preds$pref, preds$pmin)
plotRefToTarget(preds$pref, preds$pmax)

Regarding the phylogenetic “correction”, phylogeny is taken into account in every step of the calculations.  The underlying code is based on finding a phylogenetic transformation matrix, P, from a covariance matrix based on phylogeny, C, which has the property,

C = P %*% t(P)

P can be solved either by Cholesky or singular value decomposition.  Whereas PLS is generally singular value decomposition (SVD) of the cross-products between mean-centered left (X) and right (Y) matrices,

t(X) %*% Y = U %*% D %*% t(V),

the left side of the equation is updated for phylo.integration to be

t(P^-1 %*% X) %*% (P^-1 %*% Y),

where ^1 indicates matrix inversion.  This equation could be re-arranged to be t(X) %*% (t(P^-1) %*% P^-1) %*% Y = t(X) %*% C^-1 %*% Y, which is the PGLS cross-product.  The next step is important.  Generally, X-scores and Y-scores are found as X %*% U and Y %*% V (again, X and Y are centered).  But in phylo.integration, they are

X-scores = (P^-1 %*% X) %*% U
Y-scores = (P^-1 %*% Y) %*% V

This method of projection does indeed account for phylogeny, unlike phylo-PCA as proposed by Revell (2009), which uses GLS-centered (but not transformed) values for projection, such that PC scores have OLS variance rather than GLS variance.  (Whether this is most appropriate is a discussion for another day.)

I think what you might be getting at is that plotRefToTarget generally uses the mean configuration rather than a phylogenetic mean.  The example above, using an X-score of 0, implicitly uses the phylogenetic mean (more precisely, the mean of the phylogenetically transformed data) AND ALSO MORE PRECISELY the value of the reference projected on the first PLS, which is where one is attempting to visualize shape change.  (More dimensions could be considered if set up that way.)

I cannot imagine a simpler way to accomplish what I think you are trying to accomplish.  But maybe I am missing your intention?

Best,
Mike
